title: Reliability math: quorums, availability & retries
description: The numbers behind consistency and uptime claims: when a read/write quorum guarantees fresh reads, how availabilities combine in series and in parallel, what an SLO allows in downtime, how exponential backoff and jitter space out retries, the worst-case time a retry policy can burn, availability from MTBF and MTTR, and how stale an eventually consistent read can be. Availabilities are integer parts-per-million (ppm: 999,000 = 99.9%) so every answer is exact.

exercises.title: Read/write quorums
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "We replicate every key to N = 3 nodes. Writes wait for W acknowledgements and reads query R nodes. Which settings guarantee a read sees the latest write, and how many nodes can fail before we lose that?"

**Why it works.** If **R + W > N**, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one node, so some node in the read has the latest value (a *strong* read). If R + W = N they can miss each other. For a given W, the smallest strong R is **N − W + 1**. Both reads and writes still succeed while at least max(R, W) nodes are up, so the cluster tolerates **N − max(R, W)** failures.

**Your task.** Export three functions (inputs always satisfy 1 ≤ R, W ≤ N):
- `isStrongRead(n, r, w)` → `true` when r + w > n
- `minReadQuorum(n, w)` → n − w + 1
- `tolerableFailures(n, r, w)` → n − max(r, w)

**Worked example.** N = 7, W = 4 → smallest strong R = 7 − 4 + 1 = **4**; with R = W = 4 the cluster tolerates 7 − 4 = **3** failures; `isStrongRead(7, 3, 4)` → 3 + 4 = 7, not > 7 → **false**.

tests.name: N=3, R=2, W=2 -> strong (2+2 > 3)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.isStrongRead, 'function', 'export a function named isStrongRead');
assert.equal(mod.isStrongRead(3, 2, 2), true);

tests.name: N=4, R=2, W=2 -> NOT strong (boundary: R+W = N)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.isStrongRead, 'function', 'export a function named isStrongRead');
assert.equal(mod.isStrongRead(4, 2, 2), false);

tests.name: smallest strong read quorum: N=5,W=2 -> 4; N=3,W=3 -> 1
tolerable failures: N=5,R=W=3 -> 2; N=3,R=1,W=3 -> 0

exercises.explanation:
Overlap (R + W > N) is what makes reads strong; the larger quorum decides how many nodes must stay up.

For N = 5, W = 2:
- a strong read needs R + 2 > 5, i.e. R > 3
- the smallest such R is **4** = 5 − 2 + 1

For `tolerableFailures(3, 1, 3)`: writes need all 3 nodes, so max(1, 3) = 3 and 3 − 3 = **0** — one node down blocks every write. That is the trade-off of W = N.
hints: Picture the N replicas: the nodes a write touched and the nodes a read asks must share at least one node.
Strong when r + w > n. Smallest strong r = n − w + 1. Failures tolerated = n − Math.max(r, w).
return r + w > n;  /  return n - w + 1;  /  return n - Math.max(r, w);

exercises.title: Availability in series and in parallel (ppm)
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A request needs the load balancer, the app and the database, each 99.9% available. What is the end-to-end availability? And if we run two independent copies of a 99.9% service, either of which can serve, what do we get?"

**Why it works.** In **series** every component must be up, so availabilities **multiply** (always lower than the weakest link). In **parallel** the system is down only when **every** copy is down, so you multiply the *un*availabilities and subtract from 1. We use **ppm** (parts per million: 999,000 = 99.9%) so the math is integer: multiplying two ppm values gives parts-per-million², so divide by 1,000,000 after each multiplication.

**Your task.** Export two functions, each taking a non-empty array of ppm values:
- `seriesPpm(parts)` → fold left: `acc × p / 1,000,000`
- `parallelPpm(parts)` → `1,000,000 − (product of the downtimes)`, where downtime = 1,000,000 − p and the downtimes fold left the same way (`acc × d / 1,000,000`)

Inputs are chosen so every step divides exactly — no rounding needed. Multiply before you divide.

**Worked example.** series [999,000, 995,000] → 999,000 × 995,000 / 1,000,000 = **994,005** (99.4005%). parallel [990,000, 990,000] → downtimes 10,000 × 10,000 / 1,000,000 = 100 → 1,000,000 − 100 = **999,900**.

tests.name: series of two 99.9% parts -> 998,001 ppm
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.seriesPpm, 'function', 'export a function named seriesPpm');
assert.equal(mod.seriesPpm([999000,999000]), 998001);

tests.name: series of three 99% parts -> 970,299 ppm
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.seriesPpm, 'function', 'export a function named seriesPpm');
assert.equal(mod.seriesPpm([990000,990000,990000]), 970299);

tests.name: a single part is its own availability (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.seriesPpm, 'function', 'export a function named seriesPpm');
assert.equal(mod.seriesPpm([999900]), 999900);

tests.name: two 99.9% copies in parallel -> 999,999 ppm
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.parallelPpm, 'function', 'export a function named parallelPpm');
assert.equal(mod.parallelPpm([999000,999000]), 999999);

tests.name: three 90% copies in parallel -> 999,000 ppm
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.parallelPpm, 'function', 'export a function named parallelPpm');
assert.equal(mod.parallelPpm([900000,900000,900000]), 999000);

exercises.explanation:
Series multiplies availabilities; parallel multiplies downtimes. Divide by 10^6 after each multiply to stay in ppm.

For `seriesPpm([990000, 990000, 990000])`:
- start 1,000,000
- × 990,000 / 1,000,000 = 990,000
- × 990,000 / 1,000,000 = 980,100
- × 990,000 / 1,000,000 = **970,299** (97.0299%)

For `parallelPpm([900000, 900000, 900000])`: downtimes 100,000 each → 100,000 × 100,000 / 10^6 = 10,000 → × 100,000 / 10^6 = 1,000 → 1,000,000 − 1,000 = **999,000**. Three flaky 90% copies beat one 99.9% box — *if* their failures are independent.
hints: Series: all must be up → multiply availabilities. Parallel: all must be down to fail → multiply the downtimes.
series: parts.reduce((acc, p) => acc * p / 1e6, 1e6). parallel: 1e6 − parts.reduce((acc, p) => acc * (1e6 − p) / 1e6, 1e6).
const down = parts.reduce((acc, p) => (acc * (1_000_000 - p)) / 1_000_000, 1_000_000); return 1_000_000 - down;

exercises.title: Error budget: downtime allowed per month
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our SLO is 99.9% monthly availability. How many minutes of downtime is that — and we have already been down 10 minutes this month at a 99.99% SLO; how much budget is left?"

**Why it works.** The **error budget** is the unavailability you are allowed: (1 − SLO) × the period. A 30-day month has **43,200 minutes** (30 × 24 × 60). With the SLO in ppm the budget is `43,200 × (1,000,000 − ppm) / 1,000,000`. Budgets are spent in whole minutes, so **round DOWN** (Math.floor): 99.9% gives 43.2 → **43 minutes**. The remaining budget is clamped at **0** once you have overspent.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `downtimeMinutesPerMonth(availabilityPpm)` → `Math.floor(43200 × (1,000,000 − ppm) / 1,000,000)` — **round DOWN** (Math.floor)
- `budgetLeftMinutes(availabilityPpm, usedMinutes)` → `max(0, downtimeMinutesPerMonth(ppm) − usedMinutes)`

Multiply before dividing (43,200 × downtime-ppm, then ÷ 1,000,000) so the floor sees the exact value.

**Worked example.** 98% (980,000 ppm) → 43,200 × 20,000 / 1,000,000 = **864 minutes**; with 300 used → **564 left**.

tests.name: 99% -> 432 minutes a month
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.downtimeMinutesPerMonth, 'function', 'export a function named downtimeMinutesPerMonth');
assert.equal(mod.downtimeMinutesPerMonth(990000), 432);

tests.name: 99.9% -> 43.2 rounds DOWN to 43 minutes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.downtimeMinutesPerMonth, 'function', 'export a function named downtimeMinutesPerMonth');
assert.equal(mod.downtimeMinutesPerMonth(999000), 43);

tests.name: 100% -> 0 minutes (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.downtimeMinutesPerMonth, 'function', 'export a function named downtimeMinutesPerMonth');
assert.equal(mod.downtimeMinutesPerMonth(1000000), 0);

tests.name: 99.5% (216 min) with 200 used -> 16 left
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.budgetLeftMinutes, 'function', 'export a function named budgetLeftMinutes');
assert.equal(mod.budgetLeftMinutes(995000, 200), 16);

tests.name: 99.99% (4 min) with 10 used -> overspent, clamped at 0
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.budgetLeftMinutes, 'function', 'export a function named budgetLeftMinutes');
assert.equal(mod.budgetLeftMinutes(999900, 10), 0);

exercises.explanation:
Budget = month × allowed-downtime fraction, floored to whole minutes; what is left = budget − used, never negative.

For `budgetLeftMinutes(995000, 200)`:
- downtime ppm = 1,000,000 − 995,000 = 5,000
- budget = 43,200 × 5,000 / 1,000,000 = 216 minutes (exact)
- left = 216 − 200 = **16 minutes**

Useful anchors: 99% ≈ 7.2 h/month, 99.9% ≈ 43 min, 99.99% ≈ 4 min, 99.999% ≈ 26 s. Each extra nine cuts the budget tenfold.
hints: The SLO says how much of the month you must be up; the rest of the month is your downtime budget.
budget = Math.floor(43200 × (1,000,000 − ppm) / 1,000,000); left = Math.max(0, budget − used).
return Math.floor((43200 * (1_000_000 - availabilityPpm)) / 1_000_000);

exercises.title: Capped exponential backoff
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A client retries failed calls. It waits 100 ms before the first retry and doubles the wait every time, but never waits more than 10 seconds. What is the wait before retry number 4, and what is the whole schedule?"

**Why it works.** **Exponential backoff** gives a struggling service room to recover: the wait doubles each attempt, `base × 2^attempt`, so a thundering herd thins out quickly. The **cap** stops the wait growing without bound (2^20 × 100 ms would be 29 hours). Attempts are numbered from **0** (the wait before the first retry is just `base`).

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `backoffMs(baseMs, capMs, attempt)` → `Math.min(capMs, baseMs × 2^attempt)`
- `backoffSchedule(baseMs, capMs, retries)` → an array of the `retries` waits for attempts 0, 1, …, retries − 1 (empty array for 0 retries)

**Worked example.** base 50, cap 1,000: attempt 3 → 50 × 8 = **400 ms**; schedule for 6 retries → **[50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1000]** (the last would be 1,600, capped).

tests.name: attempt 0 waits exactly the base (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.backoffMs, 'function', 'export a function named backoffMs');
assert.equal(mod.backoffMs(100, 10000, 0), 100);

tests.name: attempt 4 -> 100 x 16 = 1,600 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.backoffMs, 'function', 'export a function named backoffMs');
assert.equal(mod.backoffMs(100, 10000, 4), 1600);

tests.name: attempt 5 would be 3,200 -> capped at 1,000
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.backoffMs, 'function', 'export a function named backoffMs');
assert.equal(mod.backoffMs(100, 1000, 5), 1000);

tests.name: schedule of 6 retries from 200 ms, cap 5,000
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.backoffSchedule, 'function', 'export a function named backoffSchedule');
assert.deepStrictEqual(mod.backoffSchedule(200, 5000, 6), [200,400,800,1600,3200,5000]);

tests.name: 0 retries -> empty schedule (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.backoffSchedule, 'function', 'export a function named backoffSchedule');
assert.deepStrictEqual(mod.backoffSchedule(10, 1000, 0), []);

exercises.explanation:
Double per attempt, clamp at the cap; the schedule is that formula for attempts 0..retries − 1.

For `backoffSchedule(200, 5000, 6)`:
- attempt 0: 200 × 1 = 200
- attempt 1: 200 × 2 = 400
- attempt 2: 200 × 4 = 800
- attempt 3: 200 × 8 = 1,600
- attempt 4: 200 × 16 = 3,200
- attempt 5: 200 × 32 = 6,400 → capped → 5,000
- → **[200, 400, 800, 1600, 3200, 5000]**

In production you add **jitter** to these numbers (next drill) so clients that failed together do not retry together.
hints: Each retry waits twice as long as the previous one, up to a ceiling.
backoffMs = Math.min(capMs, baseMs × 2 ** attempt); the schedule maps attempt 0..retries−1 through it.
return Array.from({ length: retries }, (_, i) => Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** i));

exercises.title: Full and equal jitter bounds
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Ten thousand clients failed at the same instant and all back off by exactly the same schedule. What goes wrong, and what range should each client pick its wait from instead?"

**Why it works.** Identical backoff makes clients retry **in lockstep**, so the retries arrive as synchronized spikes. **Jitter** spreads them out by picking a random wait inside a range built from the capped backoff `b = min(cap, base × 2^attempt)`:
- **full jitter**: anywhere in **[0, b]** — the best spread
- **equal jitter**: in **[floor(b / 2), b]** — keeps at least half the backoff, so no client retries immediately
The random pick itself is not testable, so you return the deterministic **bounds**.

**Your task.** Export two functions returning plain objects `{ min, max }` (milliseconds):
- `fullJitterBounds(baseMs, capMs, attempt)` → `{ min: 0, max: b }`
- `equalJitterBounds(baseMs, capMs, attempt)` → `{ min: Math.floor(b / 2), max: b }` — **round DOWN** (Math.floor) the half

**Worked example.** base 100, cap 2,000, attempt 2 → b = 400: full **{ min: 0, max: 400 }**, equal **{ min: 200, max: 400 }**.

tests.name: full jitter, 50 ms base, attempt 3 -> [0, 400]
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.fullJitterBounds, 'function', 'export a function named fullJitterBounds');
assert.deepStrictEqual(mod.fullJitterBounds(50, 10000, 3), {"min":0,"max":400});

tests.name: full jitter past the cap -> [0, 1000]
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.fullJitterBounds, 'function', 'export a function named fullJitterBounds');
assert.deepStrictEqual(mod.fullJitterBounds(50, 1000, 6), {"min":0,"max":1000});

tests.name: equal jitter, 50 ms base, attempt 3 -> [200, 400]
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.equalJitterBounds, 'function', 'export a function named equalJitterBounds');
assert.deepStrictEqual(mod.equalJitterBounds(50, 10000, 3), {"min":200,"max":400});

tests.name: equal jitter on an odd backoff: 25 -> [12, 25] (Math.floor)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.equalJitterBounds, 'function', 'export a function named equalJitterBounds');
assert.deepStrictEqual(mod.equalJitterBounds(25, 10000, 0), {"min":12,"max":25});

tests.name: equal jitter past the cap -> [1500, 3000]
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.equalJitterBounds, 'function', 'export a function named equalJitterBounds');
assert.deepStrictEqual(mod.equalJitterBounds(500, 3000, 4), {"min":1500,"max":3000});

exercises.explanation:
Compute the capped backoff b once; full jitter is [0, b], equal jitter is [floor(b/2), b].

For `equalJitterBounds(500, 3000, 4)`:
- uncapped = 500 × 2^4 = 8,000
- b = min(3,000, 8,000) = 3,000
- min = floor(3,000 / 2) = 1,500
- → **{ min: 1500, max: 3000 }**

A real client would then wait `min + random() × (max − min)`; testing the bounds checks your formula without any randomness.
hints: Both strategies start from the same capped exponential backoff; they differ only in where the random range starts.
b = Math.min(capMs, baseMs × 2 ** attempt); full → { min: 0, max: b }; equal → { min: Math.floor(b / 2), max: b }.
const b = Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt); return { min: Math.floor(b / 2), max: b };

exercises.title: Worst-case time of a retry policy
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Each call has a 1-second timeout; on failure we retry up to 3 times with exponential backoff from 100 ms (cap 10 s). The caller gives up after 5 seconds. In the worst case, how long can this policy run — and how many retries actually fit in the caller's deadline?"

**Why it works.** Worst case, **every** attempt runs to its timeout and every backoff is waited in full (the top of its jitter range). With `r` retries there are **r + 1 attempts** and **r waits** (before retries 1..r, i.e. backoff attempts 0..r − 1, each `min(cap, base × 2^i)`). If that total exceeds the caller's deadline, the extra retries are wasted work — the caller has already given up.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `worstCaseTotalMs(timeoutMs, retries, baseMs, capMs)` → `(retries + 1) × timeoutMs + Σ min(capMs, baseMs × 2^i)` for i = 0..retries − 1
- `maxRetriesWithin(deadlineMs, timeoutMs, baseMs, capMs)` → the **largest** `r ≥ 0` with `worstCaseTotalMs(timeoutMs, r, baseMs, capMs) ≤ deadlineMs` (inputs guarantee a single attempt fits: deadlineMs ≥ timeoutMs)

**Worked example.** timeout 200, 2 retries, base 100, cap 1,000 → 3 × 200 + (100 + 200) = **900 ms**. With a 1,000 ms deadline: r = 2 costs 900 ✓, r = 3 costs 4 × 200 + 700 = 1,500 ✗ → **2 retries**.

tests.name: 1 s timeout, 3 retries from 100 ms -> 4,700 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.worstCaseTotalMs, 'function', 'export a function named worstCaseTotalMs');
assert.equal(mod.worstCaseTotalMs(1000, 3, 100, 10000), 4700);

tests.name: no retries -> just the one timeout (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.worstCaseTotalMs, 'function', 'export a function named worstCaseTotalMs');
assert.equal(mod.worstCaseTotalMs(500, 0, 100, 1000), 500);

tests.name: 300 ms timeout, 5 retries, cap 1,000 -> 5,200 ms
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.worstCaseTotalMs, 'function', 'export a function named worstCaseTotalMs');
assert.equal(mod.worstCaseTotalMs(300, 5, 200, 1000), 5200);

tests.name: deadline exactly 4,700 ms -> 3 retries fit (boundary: <=)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxRetriesWithin, 'function', 'export a function named maxRetriesWithin');
assert.equal(mod.maxRetriesWithin(4700, 1000, 100, 10000), 3);

tests.name: deadline 2,000 ms, 1 s timeout, 500 ms base -> 0 retries fit
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxRetriesWithin, 'function', 'export a function named maxRetriesWithin');
assert.equal(mod.maxRetriesWithin(2000, 1000, 500, 5000), 0);

exercises.explanation:
Attempts × timeout plus the sum of the capped backoffs; then search upward for the largest r that still fits.

For `worstCaseTotalMs(300, 5, 200, 1000)`:
- attempts: (5 + 1) × 300 = 1,800 ms
- waits: 200 + 400 + 800 + min(1,000, 1,600) + min(1,000, 3,200) = 200 + 400 + 800 + 1,000 + 1,000 = 3,400 ms
- total = 1,800 + 3,400 = **5,200 ms**

For `maxRetriesWithin(2000, 1000, 500, 5000)`: r = 1 already costs 2 × 1,000 + 500 = 2,500 > 2,000 → **0**. Retrying here only adds load: shorten the timeout or drop the retry.
hints: Count the attempts (one more than the retries) and the waits between them (one per retry). In the worst case every one of them runs to the limit.
total = (retries + 1) × timeoutMs + Σ_{i=0}^{retries−1} Math.min(capMs, baseMs × 2 ** i). For the inverse, try r = 0, 1, 2, … while the next r still fits.
let r = 0; while (worstCaseTotalMs(timeoutMs, r + 1, baseMs, capMs) <= deadlineMs) r++; return r;

exercises.title: Availability from MTBF and MTTR
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "A node fails on average every 999 hours and takes 1 hour to repair. What is its availability — and to reach 99.9% with failures every 2,000 hours, what is the longest a repair may take?"

**Why it works.** Over one failure cycle the node is up for the **MTBF** (mean time between failures) and down for the **MTTR** (mean time to repair), so availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). In ppm: `mtbf × 1,000,000 / (mtbf + mttr)`. Rearranged for a target `t` (ppm): MTTR ≤ MTBF × (1,000,000 − t) / t. Reported in minutes and **rounded DOWN** (Math.floor) — one minute more would miss the target. This is why fast recovery (automation, small blast radius) buys as many nines as rarer failures.

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `availabilityPpm(mtbfHours, mttrHours)` → `mtbfHours × 1,000,000 / (mtbfHours + mttrHours)` (inputs divide exactly)
- `maxMttrMinutes(mtbfHours, targetPpm)` → `Math.floor(mtbfHours × 60 × (1,000,000 − targetPpm) / targetPpm)` — **round DOWN** (Math.floor)

**Worked example.** MTBF 199 h, MTTR 1 h → 199,000,000 / 200 = **995,000 ppm** (99.5%). MTBF 1,000 h at a 999,000 target → 1,000 × 60 × 1,000 / 999,000 = 60.06 → **60 minutes**.

tests.name: MTBF 999 h, MTTR 1 h -> 999,000 ppm (99.9%)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.availabilityPpm, 'function', 'export a function named availabilityPpm');
assert.equal(mod.availabilityPpm(999, 1), 999000);

tests.name: MTBF 4,999 h, MTTR 1 h -> 999,800 ppm
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.availabilityPpm, 'function', 'export a function named availabilityPpm');
assert.equal(mod.availabilityPpm(4999, 1), 999800);

tests.name: instant repair (MTTR 0) -> 1,000,000 ppm (boundary)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.availabilityPpm, 'function', 'export a function named availabilityPpm');
assert.equal(mod.availabilityPpm(720, 0), 1000000);

tests.name: MTBF 2,000 h at 99.9% -> 120.12 rounds DOWN to 120 minutes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxMttrMinutes, 'function', 'export a function named maxMttrMinutes');
assert.equal(mod.maxMttrMinutes(2000, 999000), 120);

tests.name: MTBF 720 h at 99% -> 436.36 rounds DOWN to 436 minutes
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxMttrMinutes, 'function', 'export a function named maxMttrMinutes');
assert.equal(mod.maxMttrMinutes(720, 990000), 436);

exercises.explanation:
Availability is the up share of a fail-repair cycle; the inverse solves that ratio for MTTR.

For `maxMttrMinutes(2000, 999000)`:
- MTBF in minutes = 2,000 × 60 = 120,000
- allowed downtime share = (1,000,000 − 999,000) / 999,000 = 1,000 / 999,000
- MTTR ≤ 120,000 × 1,000 / 999,000 = 120,000,000 / 999,000 = 120.12…
- Math.floor → **120 minutes**

Check: availabilityPpm with MTBF 120,000 min and MTTR 120 min = 120,000,000,000 / 120,120 ≈ 999,001 ppm ≥ 999,000 ✓.
hints: Think of one cycle: up for MTBF, down for MTTR. Availability is the fraction of that cycle spent up.
availabilityPpm = mtbf × 1e6 / (mtbf + mttr). From A = mtbf/(mtbf+mttr) ≥ t you get mttr ≤ mtbf × (1e6 − t) / t; convert hours to minutes (× 60) and Math.floor.
return Math.floor((mtbfHours * 60 * (1_000_000 - targetPpm)) / targetPpm);

exercises.title: How stale can a replicated read be?
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "With N = 3 replicas, R = 1 and W = 1, replication lag is up to 250 ms and we serve 2,000 reads per second. How stale can a read be, and how many reads after a write might see old data?"

**Why it works.** When **R + W > N** the read quorum always overlaps the latest write, so a read is never stale: **0 ms**. Otherwise a read can land on a replica that has not caught up yet, so it can be as stale as the **replication lag**. During that window every read is at risk, so the reads that may see stale data after one write = `readQps × staleMs / 1000` (Little's-law style: rate × time).

**Your task.** Export two functions:
- `maxStaleReadMs(n, r, w, lagMs)` → `0` when r + w > n, else `lagMs`
- `staleWindowReads(n, r, w, lagMs, readQps)` → `readQps × maxStaleReadMs(...) / 1000` (inputs divide exactly)

**Worked example.** N = 3, R = 1, W = 1, lag 200 ms, 500 reads/s → stale up to **200 ms**; 500 × 200 / 1,000 = **100 reads** at risk per write.

tests.name: N=3, R=2, W=2 overlap -> never stale (0 ms)
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxStaleReadMs, 'function', 'export a function named maxStaleReadMs');
assert.equal(mod.maxStaleReadMs(3, 2, 2, 150), 0);

tests.name: N=3, R=1, W=2 (R+W = N, boundary) -> up to the lag
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxStaleReadMs, 'function', 'export a function named maxStaleReadMs');
assert.equal(mod.maxStaleReadMs(3, 1, 2, 150), 150);

tests.name: N=5, R=1, W=1 -> up to the 80 ms lag
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.maxStaleReadMs, 'function', 'export a function named maxStaleReadMs');
assert.equal(mod.maxStaleReadMs(5, 1, 1, 80), 80);

tests.name: R=W=1 of 3, 250 ms lag, 2,000 reads/s -> 500 reads at risk
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.staleWindowReads, 'function', 'export a function named staleWindowReads');
assert.equal(mod.staleWindowReads(3, 1, 1, 250, 2000), 500);

tests.name: N=5, R=W=3 overlap -> 0 reads at risk
tests.code:
assert.equal(typeof mod.staleWindowReads, 'function', 'export a function named staleWindowReads');
assert.equal(mod.staleWindowReads(5, 3, 3, 250, 2000), 0);

exercises.explanation:
Overlap means fresh; no overlap means stale up to the lag; reads at risk = rate × stale window.

For `staleWindowReads(3, 1, 1, 250, 2000)`:
- R + W = 2, not > 3 → stale window = 250 ms
- reads at risk = 2,000 × 250 / 1,000 = **500 reads**

Raising W to 3 (R + W = 4 > 3) makes it 0 — at the price of every write waiting for the slowest replica. Name that trade-off out loud.
hints: Reuse the quorum rule: when read and write sets must overlap, there is no stale window at all.
maxStaleReadMs = (r + w > n) ? 0 : lagMs; staleWindowReads = readQps × maxStaleReadMs / 1000.
return (readQps * maxStaleReadMs(n, r, w, lagMs)) / 1000;
